title: Effective sample size counted in events: right direction, no gain over ESS times the event rate
question: With rare binary outcomes, does an effective sample size counted in events (EESS) predict when a MAIC interval fails better than the reported ESS multiplied by the event rate, and in which direction do the two diverge?
answer: EESS is the reciprocal of the sandwich variance of a weighted log odds, and it differs from ESS times the event rate by E_w[w]E_w[p]/E_w[wp]: below 1 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, above 1 on low-risk ones (the design had the direction reversed). As a predictor of failure the two were equivalent (AUROC 0.839 and 0.858) and ESS alone was poor (0.662). Their predictive value comes from zero-event analyses; once an estimate exists, non-coverage is near nominal and neither predicts it.
findings: Median EESS / (ESS p): 0.47 to 0.79 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, 1.28 to 2.40 on low-risk patients, 1.00 to 1.03 when the shift is in a non-prognostic covariate.
AUROC for failure (no estimate or non-coverage) over 108,000 analyses: EESS 0.839, ESS x event rate 0.858, ESS 0.662; the registered rule, requiring EESS to be better by 0.05, is refuted.
No estimate (an arm with no events) in up to 86% of analyses at risk 0.005 and 300 per arm.
Among analyses with an estimate, non-coverage was 5.7% and the diagnostics' AUROC 0.54 to 0.59 (exploratory).
not_answered: One prognostic covariate, MAIC on means; the penalized, Firth, Bayesian and fail-closed estimators were not run, and unanchored comparisons and multivariable separation are outside the design. Peer review has not been done.
design: Binary-outcome MAIC with one prognostic covariate among three, 108 scenarios crossing event risk (0.005 to 0.1), size and direction of the target shift relative to risk, sample size and effect; EESS, ESS times the event rate and ESS as per-analysis predictors of failure.
estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C; failure of its interval
